titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Hymn to Ra at his rising
part: Hymn to Ra at his rising (Plate 1)
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plate I. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 1–5; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: A hymn to the sun-god Ra as he rises in the east, spoken by Ani: he greets Ra as Khepri, calls on the gods to praise him, tells of the sun's daily course and the overthrow of his enemies, and asks to see the sun and the moon, to come forth as a living ba and to travel in the sun's bark. It is the first text of the papyrus, on Plate 1, written beside the picture of Ani and his wife Thuthu raising their hands in adoration.

sentences.l: adoring · Ra · when · rises · he · in · the-horizon · eastern · of · the-sky
sentences.i: Adoring Ra when he rises in the eastern horizon of the sky.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes this title in red, except for the name of Ra and the last two words, nt pt 'of the sky', which stand in black. dwꜣ 'adore, praise' is the star (dwꜣ) with a man raising his arms in worship and the papyrus roll; here it is the infinitive, naming the act: 'adoring Ra'. rꜥ 'Ra' is mouth r and arm ꜥ, with the sun-disk, its stroke and the seated god as classifiers. ḫft 'when' (placenta ḫ, horned viper f, loaf t) is a preposition, 'in front of, at the time of', that can also stand before a verb. wbn·f is the sḏm·f, the plain form of the verb with its subject joined on: wbn 'rise, shine' (quail chick w, foot b, water n, the sun as classifier) and ·f 'he', the horned viper. Every suffix pronoun works this way, on verbs and on nouns alike: ·f 'he, his', ·s 'she, her, it', ·k 'you, your', ·i 'I, my', ·sn 'they, their'. m 'in' is written with Aa15, an object of uncertain nature that writes m. ꜣḫt 'horizon' is the sun between two hills, with t and the house as classifier: the place where the sun comes up and goes down. iꜣbtt 'eastern' is the emblem of the East with b, t, t and the hill-country sign; its feminine ending agrees with ꜣḫt. nt is the genitive 'of' in its feminine form (water n, loaf t); pt 'sky' is p, t and the sign of the sky. The hymn greets the sun at dawn.

sentences.i: By the Osiris, the scribe of the god's offerings of all the gods, Ani. He says:
sentences.n: in, in red, is the particle that names the one who acts, 'by': here the one who speaks the hymn. Its second sign is doubtful in Budge's type, a pot-like sign with a spiral top, taken as W25, the sign that writes in, with the reed i as its complement. Budge reads àn and gives 'behold'; in is read here because it is the usual way to name the speaker after a title, as in ḏd in N 'said by N'. Wsir Ani, 'the Osiris Ani': the eye (ir) printed above the seat (ws), with the seated god. The dead man bears the name of Osiris, the god who died and lived again, because he hopes to live again as the god did; the phrase stands before his name all through the papyrus. sš 'scribe' is the scribe's palette, water-pot and pen. The next two groups are one title, ḥtp-nṯr 'the god's offerings', the offerings of a temple: the flag nṯr 'god' is written first out of respect though it is read last, and the offering table ḥtp follows with t and p as complements. Budge prints them as two words; they are joined here. n is the genitive 'of'; nṯrw 'the gods' writes the flag three times for the plural, and nbw 'all' (the basket nb with plural strokes) agrees with it. ꜣny 'Ani' is vulture ꜣ, water n and two reeds (y) with the seated man; the three small strokes under ꜣ-n belong to the usual writing of his name and are not read. ḏd·f 'he says' (cobra ḏ, hand d, ·f), in red again, brings in the speech. Ani's title makes him the scribe who kept the record of the offerings given to the gods.

sentences.l: greetings · to-your-face · having-come · you · as · Khepri · Khepri · as · creator · of-the-gods
sentences.i: Hail to you, who have come as Khepri — Khepri, the creator of the gods!
sentences.n: Ani's speech to the sun begins; ind ḥr·k is in red. ind 'hail, greetings' is the reed i and a shaft with a cross-bar (the sign nḏ, uncertain in the print) with the cobra ḏ as complement; ḥr·k is the face ḥr with its stroke and the basket ·k 'you, your' — literally 'greetings to your face'. Budge prints the two as one group; they are split here into the interjection and ḥr·k. ii·ṯi 'you have come' is the stative, the form that describes a state reached: the reed-leaves ii with a reed as complement, two strokes often written in this verb, the walking legs, and the ending ·ṯi 'you' (tethering rope ṯ and reed). After ind ḥr·k the stative gives 'you who have come'. m 'as' is the owl. ḫpri 'Khepri' (Budge: Kheperà) is the scarab beetle ḫpr with r as complement, a reed i and the seated god: the sun as he comes into being at dawn, his name made from ḫpr 'come into being'. The papyrus writes the name twice; the second Khepri begins a phrase of its own. qmꜣ 'create' is a small triangle taken as q (not clear in the print), the sickle mꜣ with m as complement, and a long curved stick as classifier (approximated in the type); after m it is a participle used as a noun, 'creator'. The first thought of the hymn: the rising sun is Khepri, who made the gods.

sentences.l: appear · you · rise · you · shines · mother · your · having-appeared · you · as · king · of-the-gods
sentences.i: You appear in glory and rise, and your mother shines; you have appeared as king of the gods.
sentences.n: ḫꜥ·k and wbn·k are two sḏm·f forms, 'you appear, you rise', with ·k 'you'. ḫꜥ 'appear in glory' is the sun rising over a hill (ḫꜥ) with the arm ꜥ as complement: the word for a king appearing on his throne or a god coming out in procession. wbn as in the title. psd 'shine' is p, the bolt s and the hand d, with the sun shedding rays and the sun-disk as classifiers; it is spelled with the hand d where older writing has the cobra (psḏ), a common later spelling. No suffix follows it, so as it stands it is a sḏm·f whose subject is the noun after it, mwt·k 'your mother': 'your mother shines', the sky growing bright as the sun comes up. Budge takes it as 'making bright thy mother', with mwt·k as object; that needs a form that is not written (a participle or an infinitive), and the plain reading is kept. mwt 'mother' is the vulture (mwt) with t, then ·k. ḫꜥ·ṯi is ḫꜥ again, with the papyrus roll and the stative ending ·ṯi 'you': 'you having appeared'. m nswt nṯrw 'as king of the gods': nswt 'king' is the sedge alone. The papyrus writes the flag with t and plural strokes, the spelling of nṯrwt 'goddesses'; read nṯrw 'gods', as the phrase nswt nṯrw 'king of the gods' requires, with Budge. The mother is the sky-goddess Nut, named in the next line: each morning the sun is born from her.

sentences.l: makes · for-you · mother · Nut · her-two-arms · in · the-doing · of-greeting
sentences.i: Mother Nut sets her two arms for you in the gesture of welcome.
sentences.n: Budge prints àri-nek as one group; it is split here into the verb and n·k 'for you' (water n, the preposition 'to, for', and ·k). The verb is the eye ir 'make, do' with two reeds (y), a sḏm·f whose subject is a noun, mwt nwt 'mother Nut'; the short n·k comes before the subject, as short words do in Egyptian. What the two reeds mark is not certain: in verbs like iri the prospective sḏm·f, the form of wish and of what is to come, is often written with y (iry·f), which would give 'may mother Nut set …'; the plain statement is kept as fitting the description around it. mwt 'mother' has no suffix this time; nwt 'Nut' is the pot nw with t, the sign of the sky and the seated woman. ꜥwy·s 'her two arms' is the object: the arm ꜥ written twice with a stroke between, w and two strokes y for the ending -wy, and the bolt ·s 'her'. This is the dual, the form for exactly two of a thing: -wy on masculine nouns, -ty on feminine ones. m irt nyny 'in the act of greeting': irt is the infinitive of iri, 'making, doing' (eye and t), and nyny 'greet, welcome' is n and two strokes y written twice, with a man holding his arms out (approximated in the type) as classifier. Nut is the sky; she receives the sun with open arms as he rises.

sentences.l: receives · you · Manu · in · peace · embraces · you · Maat · at · the-two-times
sentences.i: Manu receives you in peace, and Maat embraces you at both times of the day.
sentences.n: Two sentences of one build: verb, object pronoun, subject. When the object is a pronoun it comes straight after the verb, before a noun subject. šsp 'receive' is a low fence-like sign (šsp) with p as complement, then the low flat sign printed as U15 (the sledge, which writes tm) where a classifier is expected; it is taken as a classifier and not read. Budge prints šsp tw as one group; it is split here into the verb and tw 'you' (loaf t, quail chick w), the dependent pronoun, the form a pronoun takes as the object of a verb. The same split is made in ḥpt tw. mꜣnw 'Manu' is the sickle mꜣ with the pot nw written three times and the hill-country sign: the mountain of the west where the sun sets. m ḥtp 'in peace': ḥtp is the offering table with t and p as complements. ḥpt 'embrace' is wick ḥ, p, t and the two embracing arms as classifier. mꜣꜥt 'Maat', here the goddess, is the seated goddess with a feather on her head alone. r trwy 'at the two times': tr 'time, season' is t, r, a reed for the y of the dual, the plant-stem sign tr, and two sun-disks for the two times of day, morning and evening. Manu takes in the sun at evening, and Maat, the right order of the world, holds him through his whole course.

sentences.l: may-give · he · glory · power · with · vindication
sentences.i: May he grant glory and power, with vindication,
sentences.n: The language of the offering formula: what the god is asked to give the dead. di·f 'may he give' is the arm holding a conical loaf (di, the sign of giving) and ·f; the sḏm·f here expresses a wish, and 'he' is Ra. ꜣḫ 'glory, effective power' is the crested ibis (ꜣḫ) with the placenta ḫ as complement: the state of the ꜣḫ, the dead who has become a shining and effective spirit. wsr 'power, strength' is the staff-head sign wsr with s as complement. m 'with' is Aa15. mꜣꜥ-ḫrw, the plinth (mꜣꜥ) above the oar (ḫrw 'voice'), is 'true of voice': one whose words were found true when he was judged, and so vindicated. It is said of every dead person who has passed the judgement, and it follows Ani's name all through the papyrus; here it is used as a noun, 'vindication'. Budge's type shows the plinth without the sickle mꜣ that often stands before it.

sentences.l: a-coming-forth · as · a-ba · living · to · see · Horakhty
sentences.i: and a coming forth as a living ba to see Horakhty,
sentences.n: prt 'coming forth' is the infinitive of pri 'go out' — the house pr with r as complement, the t of this infinitive, and the walking legs — used as a noun, the next thing asked for. m 'as' is the owl. bꜣ 'ba' is the saddle-billed stork (jabiru), which writes bꜣ; the small pot with a flame before it in Budge's type (approximated as the incense bowl R7) is not read. Budge's footnote mark stands at the bird's upper right. The ba is the power of a person to move and take form after death, drawn as a bird with a human head that leaves the tomb by day. ꜥnḫy 'living' is the ankh (ꜥnḫ) with n and ḫ as complements and two reeds (y): the participle 'who lives, living', agreeing with bꜣ. The participle of ꜥnḫ has no regular ending -y, and what the reeds mark here is not clear; Budge too reads ānχi. r mꜣꜣ 'to see': r with an infinitive gives the purpose. mꜣꜣ is the eye with the sickle mꜣ printed hooked onto it as one sign. ḥr-ꜣḫty 'Horakhty', 'Horus of the horizon' (Budge: Ḥeru-χuti), is the falcon ḥr with a second sign that the type gives as two small rounded shapes one above the other, coded as the horizon sign (N27), an approximation; the reading is Budge's and fits the falcon. He is the sun standing above the horizon.

sentences.n: n kꜣ n N 'for the ka of N' closes the offering formula by naming the one for whom all this is asked. The first n is the preposition 'to, for'; the second is the genitive 'of'. kꜣ 'ka' is the two raised arms (kꜣ) with its stroke: the life-force that is born with a person, lives on after death, and receives the offerings. Wsir sš ꜣny as before; here the figure after Ani's name is a man seated on a block seat holding something before him (coded A51, the seated noble). mꜣꜥ-ḫrw is spelled more fully this time: the sickle mꜣ and the arm ꜥ before the plinth mꜣꜥ, then the oar ḫrw. ḫr 'before, with' (placenta ḫ, mouth r) is the preposition used of persons, especially a god or a king: Ani is vindicated in the presence of Osiris, the judge of the dead. Wsir is now written with the seat above the eye, the seat drawn like a couchant animal in the type (an approximation).

sentences.l: says · he · O · gods · all · of · the-Mansion-of-the-Ba · who-judge · sky · earth · in · the-balance · who-give · food · provisions
sentences.i: He says: O all you gods of the Mansion of the Ba, who judge sky and earth in the balance, who give food and provisions,
sentences.n: ḏd·f 'he says', in red again, opens a second speech, to the gods. i 'O' is the reed with a man raising one arm to call. nṯrw nbw 'all the gods' as before; nw is the plural form of the genitive 'of' (the pot nw and a stroke), agreeing with nṯrw. ḥwt-bꜣ 'the Mansion of the Ba' (Budge: Ḥet-ba) is the enclosure ḥwt with the ba-bird inside it, and the same small pot before the bird as in bꜣ above: a temple, by its name a sanctuary of the ba. wḏꜥw 'who judge' is the sign wḏꜥ (Aa21) with its stroke: a participle — a verb used as an adjective or a noun, 'one who judges' — here plural, agreeing with the gods. pt tꜣ 'sky (and) earth' are two nouns side by side with no 'and'; tꜣ is the strip of land with grains of sand beneath. m mḫꜣt 'in the balance': mḫꜣt is the balance-scale alone. ddw 'who give' is the giving arm written twice, the participle of rdi for repeated or lasting action. kꜣw 'food' has the same signs as kꜣ 'ka' (arms and stroke), in the sense 'sustenance'. The papyrus writes ḏ-f with the pintail duck (sꜣ) where the vulture ꜣ is expected; read ḏfꜣw 'provisions', the usual partner of kꜣw. The gods are hailed as the judges of the world and the givers of its food.

sentences.l: Tatenen · the-One · who-made · mankind · the-cake-offerings-of-the-gods · of-the-south · the-north · the-west · the-east
sentences.i: Tatenen, the One, who made mankind and the cake-offerings of the gods of the south, the north, the west and the east!
sentences.n: tꜣ-ṯnn 'Tatenen' (Budge: Ta-tu-nen), the god of the land that rose out of the waters at the beginning, is spelled with the land sign tꜣ, t and w, two tall rushes and two water-lines n, and the seated god with two plumes (approximated in the type); the rushes are taken as n, and the w, not in the usual spelling, is kept in the reading as written. wꜥ 'the One' is the harpoon wꜥ with its stroke and ꜥ as complement: the god who was alone before creation. ir 'who made' is the participle of iri, the eye alone. tmmw 'mankind, all people' is t, the sledge tm, the owl for the second m (Budge: tememu), w, a man and a woman and a stroke. Budge prints paut and neteru as two words; they are joined here as pꜣwt-nṯrw 'the cake-offerings of the gods', the phrase of the declarations of Spell 125: pꜣwt is a round loaf (approximated as X6) with t, then the three flags. The same loaf writes pꜣwt 'primeval time' (pꜣwty 'the primeval one'), and 'who made mankind and the primeval gods' is also possible; the choice is not certain. rsy 'the south' (the sedge plant rs, two strokes y), mḥtt 'the north' (the papyrus clump mḥ, t, t), imntt 'the west' and iꜣbtt 'the east' (the emblems of the West and the East with t, t and the hill-country sign) name the four quarters and follow nṯrw directly as genitives: 'the gods of the south, the north …'. They are not adjectives agreeing with nṯrw, which would be masculine plural (rsyw, mḥtyw …); mḥtt, imntt and iꜣbtt are the feminine nouns for the regions. The small wedge after rs and mḥ (approximated) is taken as a classifier. Tatenen is praised as maker both of people and of the food of the gods in all four quarters.

sentences.i: Give praise to Ra, lord of the sky, the sovereign — life, prosperity, health! — who made the gods.
sentences.n: imi 'give!' is the imperative that serves rdi 'give': the reed i and the owl m, then a ligature of two forearms, the upper one ending in an upright hand, which Budge's type gives as two arms (coded D36 D36, an approximation); it is taken as the arm of giving written as a classifier, and not read. The gods are told to give. iꜣw 'praise' (reed, vulture, quail chick, and a man with raised arms). n 'to' is the preposition. nb pt 'lord of the sky' is the basket nb followed by its noun as a direct genitive, with no 'of' written. iṯy 'sovereign' is the reed, the rope ṯ and two reeds, with a seated king holding a sceptre (approximated) as classifier; Budge reads àθi. The word is usually spelled with t; the papyrus has ṯ. ꜥnḫ wḏꜣ snb 'life, prosperity, health' is the wish written after a king's name or title: the ankh, the fire-drill ḏꜣ standing for wḏꜣ 'be sound, prosper', and the bolt s for snb 'be healthy' — each word cut short to one sign. ir nṯrw 'who made the gods' is the participle of iri, the eye alone, and the three flags. Ra is hailed as the king of the world, with the very wish a scribe wrote after Pharaoh's name.

sentences.i: May you adore him in his beautiful form, in his appearing in the Adjet-bark.
sentences.n: dwꜣ·tn 'may you adore' is the star dwꜣ with the man raising his arms, and ·tn 'you' (plural), written with loaf t, water n and plural strokes; a sḏm·f with a suffix after an imperative carries the command on as a wish. sw 'him' is the sedge sw with w as complement, the dependent pronoun as object. irw 'form, appearance' is the eye ir with a standing, wrapped figure and the papyrus roll as classifiers, then ·f 'his'; nfr 'beautiful' (the heart and windpipe nfr, with f and r as complements) comes after the noun and its suffix, as Egyptian adjectives do. m ḫꜥ·f 'in his appearing': ḫꜥ is now the infinitive, with ·f as its subject. The bark is spelled with the netting-needle sign ꜥḏ (V26), the hand d standing for ḏ, two t's and a boat (approximated); read ꜥḏt, Budge's āṭet, which he takes as the bark in which the sun sails by day. The sign also has the value ꜥnḏ, and the sun's morning bark is often named mꜥnḏt; no m is written here, and ꜥḏt follows the signs and Budge. The sun crosses the sky by boat, as an Egyptian crossed the Nile.

sentences.i: Those above adore you; those below adore you.
sentences.n: Two short sentences built like šsp tw mꜣnw: verb, the pronoun tw 'you', and the subject; the 'you' is the sun again. tw is the loaf t with the curl w (the hieratic form of the quail chick). Budge prints dwꜣ tw as one group each time; they are split here. ḥryw 'those who are above' is the face ḥr with r as complement, the sign of the sky and plural strokes; ẖryw 'those who are below' is the belly-and-udder sign ẖr with r and a stroke. Both are nisbas: adjectives made by adding -y to a preposition or noun (ḥr 'upon' → ḥry 'who is upon'; ẖr 'under' → ẖry 'who is under'), here used as plural nouns. Between them they take in all beings, in the sky and beneath the earth.

sentences.l: write · for-you · Thoth · Maat · daily(?) · day · every
sentences.i: Thoth and Maat write for you daily(?), every day.
sentences.n: sš 'write' is the scribe's palette with the papyrus roll; Budge reads it ān, but the palette is the regular sign of sš, as in the rubric of Spell 125. It is a sḏm·f with two subjects side by side and no 'and': ḏḥwty 'Thoth' (the ibis on its standard) and mꜣꜥt 'Maat' (sickle mꜣ, arm ꜥ, t and the seated goddess). n·k 'for you' stands before them, as short words do. What they write is not said; Thoth is the scribe of the gods, and both stand beside the sun in his bark, as the hymn says below. The next word is doubtful: Budge reads ment 'daily', but the type shows the sun with rays standing on the arm ꜥ, then n and t, with no sign for m. It is read mnt 'daily' after Budge, with that doubt. rꜥ nb 'every day' is rꜥ 'sun, day' (mouth, arm, sun-disk and stroke) and nb 'every', which follows its noun.

sentences.i: Your enemy is given over to the fire; the Rebel has fallen.
sentences.n: Two sentences of a noun and a verb in the stative, the form that describes the state the subject is in. ḫfty·k 'your enemy' is placenta ḫ, f and t (the y of ḫfty is not written), with a snake as classifier of hostile beings, and ·k. rdi·w 'given' is mouth r and the giving arm with the curl w, the ending of the 3rd person masculine stative ('he is …ed'). n sḏt 'to the fire': sḏt is the crossed sticks sḏ, t and a flame on a brazier (approximated in the type). sbiw 'the Rebel' (Budge: Sebàu) is s, b, reed i and w with the snake: a serpent enemy of the sun. ḫr 'fallen' (placenta ḫ, mouth r, and the falling man) is the stative of ḫr 'fall', with no ending written. The enemies of the sun are burnt and thrown down each morning so that he can rise.

sentences.i: His arms are bound, and Ra has taken away his legs.
sentences.n: ꜥwy·f 'his two arms' is the arm written twice, with a stroke between, and ·f; the dual ending is not spelled out this time. qꜣs 'bound' is q, vulture ꜣ, w and s, then the crossed sticks and the low flat sign printed as U15 as classifiers (U15 stands where a classifier of force might be expected, as in šsp above); it is taken as the stative, like ḫr before it, and the w before s is not accounted for. nḥm·n is the sḏm·n·f, the form of completed action, 'has taken away': the verb nḥm (water n, a bowl-shaped sign coded W10 that the type gives for the sign ḥm, m as complement, U15 again) and then the n that marks the form, before the subject. Budge prints this n as a word of its own (en); it is joined to the verb here. The subject is rꜥ, written now with the seated god with the sun-disk alone. rdw·f 'his legs' is the walking legs written three times, the plural, and ·f. Bound and lamed, the Rebel can no longer move against the sun.

sentences.n: The prayer turns to Ani himself. ḥtp·k 'may you be content, gracious' is ḥtp (offering table, t, p) with ·k: the sḏm·f of wish. n·i 'to me, with me' is water n and the seated man ·i, the suffix 'I, me, my'. mꜣꜣ·i 'that I may see' is the sickle and eye with ·i; after a wish, the sḏm·f's that follow say what it is for. nfrw·k 'your beauty' is the heart-and-windpipe nfr written three times — the plural, used for an abstract noun — and ·k. wḏꜣ·i 'that I may go about' is quail chick w, fire-drill ḏꜣ and the seated man. sentences.i: May I strike the donkey, may I cut up the Rebel; I have destroyed Apep in his moment.
sentences.n: ḥw·i 'may I strike' is wick ḥ with two classifiers of force, a man striking with a stick and the forearm holding a stick, and ·i. ꜥꜣ 'donkey' is the column ꜥꜣ with ꜥ as complement, a flat sign with a rolled end (approximated as D52), w and the donkey. bḥn·i 'may I cut up' is b, ḥ, n, the low flat sign printed as U15 in place of a classifier, and ·i. The donkey and the Rebel are enemies of the sun. The next verb is sḥtm 'destroy', the causative (s-) of ḥtm 'perish': the type gives s, ḥ, a seat (coded Q1; no value of it fits, and it is not read), Aa15 m and a long-billed bird (approximated) as classifier, so the t is not written; Budge reads se-ḥetem. Then come n and ·i: this is the sḏm·n·f, 'I have destroyed', and the same form returns in mꜣꜣ·n·i and šsp·n·i below. Budge carries 'may I' through; the completed sense of the form is kept here, but a change of form inside a run of wishes is odd, and the scribe may have meant wishes throughout. The form can also stand as a clause of circumstance tied to the wishes before it, 'when I have destroyed Apep'; either way the n marks a completed act, and a sḏm·n·f is never a wish. ꜥꜣpp 'Apep' (Budge: Āpep) is the column ꜥꜣ (approximated) and p twice: the great serpent who attacks the sun's bark. ꜣt 'moment' is the leopard's head ꜣt (an animal head not clear in the print) with t and the sun as classifier of time: 'in his moment', when he strikes.

sentences.i: I have seen the abdju-fish when its moment came, and the inet-fish … and the inet in its pool.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes mꜣꜣ·n with no seated man; read mꜣꜣ·n·i 'I have seen' (sickle, eye and the n of the sḏm·n·f), as the run of first-person verbs requires; the suffix ·i is often left unwritten in copies of this time, so this is hardly a slip. Budge's type gives the first sign of the next word as a loop with bars on a long stick, like the ankh (coded S34, an approximation); read ꜣbḏw, the abdju-fish: the sign expected is ꜣb (U23), with b as complement, the mountain ḏw and a fish. Whether the papyrus or only the type has the odd form cannot be told from the print. Budge too reads àbṭu. sp·f 'its time' is s and p with the threshing floor as classifier, and ·f; ḫpr 'come into being, happen' (scarab, r) follows. A noun that carries a suffix cannot take a direct genitive after it (that would be sp ḫpr·f), so ḫpr is not 'of coming into being': it is read as the stative after a noun subject, 'its occasion having come about', a clause of circumstance, 'when its time came'. The phrase is not certain. int 'the inet-fish' is reed i, a fish, n, t and a second, plumper fish. Budge's footnote says that a papyrus at Leiden has more words here; Ani's copy is short, and the bolt s after it stands alone and is not understood. Then int again, now with a boat as classifier, m mr·s 'in its pool': mr 'canal, pool' is the canal sign with a stroke and a small wedge, and ·s 'its' (the bolt). The two fish belong to the sun's voyage; to see them is to travel with the bark.

sentences.n: šsp·n·i 'I have taken hold of': the šsp sign alone, the n of the sḏm·n·f, and, in place of the seated man, a single stroke, which can stand for the suffix ·i; Budge reads seśep-nà. ḥꜣtw is the forepart of a lion (ḥꜣt 'front') with t and the curl w written twice: the front or prow of a boat, perhaps the prow-rope by which it is hauled; the exact sense is not certain. m 'in' (the owl). sktt, the Sektet-bark (Budge: sektet), is the bolt s, the basket k, t, t and a boat with a cabin. pḥwyt 'the hinder part, the stern' is the lion's hindquarters pḥ with w, two reeds, t and w: the feminine noun from pḥwy 'rear'. m ꜥḏt 'in the Adjet-bark', as on line 8; here the first sign is an oval with crossing ends (coded Z9 from the type, an approximation of the netting-needle sign). Budge takes the Sektet as the sun's bark of the evening and the āṭet as its bark of the morning: holding the front of one and the back of the other, Ani travels with the sun through day and night.

sentences.l: may-give · he · [see] · I · the-Disk · behold · the-Moon · without · ceasing · day · every
sentences.i: May he grant that I see the Disk and behold the Moon without ceasing, every day,
sentences.n: di·f 'may he give, may he grant', as in line 4; a sḏm·f after rdi says what is granted: 'that I see'. The verb is restored: the type prints only a faint seated man in outline (Budge's way of showing damage), taken as the suffix ·i, and no sign of the verb itself; Budge supplies [maa], mꜣꜣ 'see', in his transliteration from the sense. The reading gives mꜣꜣ·i, but only ·i is analysed, since the verb has no sign here. iṯn 'the Disk' (reed i, rope ṯ, water n, sun-disk) is the visible disk of the sun; the word is usually spelled with t. dgg 'look at, behold' is hand d and the jar-stand g written twice, with the eye as classifier; Budge reads ṭeḳeḳ. No subject is written after it: it is taken as a second sḏm·f after di·f, parallel to mꜣꜣ·i, with ·i unwritten, as often. The papyrus writes i-ḥ with the seated god wearing disk and crescent; read iꜥḥ 'the Moon', with the arm ꜥ left out. n ꜣbw 'without ceasing': n (the arms spread, with n) before a noun is 'without', and ꜣbw 'ceasing' is the sign ꜣb (U23, approximated) with b as complement and w. rꜥ nb 'every day'. The dead man asks to see the sun by day and the moon by night, for ever.

sentences.l: may-go-forth · the-ba · to · walk-about · to · place · every · which-wishes · it
sentences.i: and may (my) ba go forth to walk about to every place it wishes.
sentences.n: pr 'go forth' (the house pr with r and the walking legs) is a sḏm·f whose subject is bꜣ 'the ba' (the stork, with the small pot before it again). Budge reads ba-à 'my soul', but no sign for 'my' is written, and the English puts it in brackets. r swtwt 'to walk about': swtwt 'stroll, walk about' is spelled s, t, w, t with two leg-signs as classifiers and a further t and w, in the order the type gives them, with Budge's line numeral 19 printed inside the word; Budge reads setut-tu. r bw nb 'to every place': bw 'place' is foot b with its stroke. mrr·f is a relative form of mri 'love, wish' — a verb form that works as a relative clause, 'which he loves, which he wishes': the hoe mr, r and a second r (the doubled r marks this form), and ·f, referring to the ba. That the ba may go out of the tomb and come back as it wishes is one of the commonest wishes in the Book of the Dead.

sentences.l: may-be-called · my-name · may-be-found · it · upon · the-board · of-reverting · offerings
sentences.i: May my name be called out, and may it be found upon the board for the reversion of offerings.
sentences.n: nis·tw 'may (my name) be called out' is the passive sḏm·tw·f of nis 'call, summon': water n, reed i, bolt s, then t — the tw of the passive written short — and a man raising an arm to call. rn·i 'my name' is mouth r and water n with the man with hand to mouth, and ·i. gm·f is the ibis gm with m and the papyrus roll, and ·f 'it', the name. It is the passive sḏm·f, 'may it be found': this passive takes a suffix pronoun as its subject and need write no ending, so nothing is missing (read actively, 'it finds', the verb would have no object). Budge too takes it as passive. m 'upon' (Aa15). ḫt here is the branch ḫt with t and a stroke: 'wood, a wooden board'. The papyrus writes b-w-d; read wdb: the foot b, the quail chick w and the hand d stand in that order, with a flat bar (approximated) and the papyrus roll; Budge reads uṭeb. wdb ḫt 'the turning over of offerings' is the passing on of offerings from the god's altar to the dead; ḫt 'things, offerings' is placenta ḫ, t, a mat with a loaf (approximated) and plural strokes. What the board is — an offering table, or a list of names — is not certain; m-ḫt 'after', written with the same signs, is another possible reading of m ḫt.

sentences.i: May offerings be given to me, set before me, like the followers of Horus.
sentences.n: di·tw 'may there be given' is the giving arm with t and the curl w, the passive sḏm·tw·f; Budge's line numeral 23 is printed inside this group, which he prints as one word with n·i 'to me'. It is split here into the verb and n·i. ḥtpw 'offerings' is the offering table ḥtp with a sign like a tied roll (Y1) and three small circles, the plural of things. m-bꜣḥ·i 'in my presence, before me' is Aa15 m and the phallus sign bꜣḥ (approximated in the type), the compound preposition m-bꜣḥ, with a single stroke for ·i, as in šsp·n·i. mi 'like' is the milk-jug mi. šmsw ḥr 'the followers of Horus': šmsw is the šms sign (a bundle on a staff), s, the walking legs and plural strokes, and ḥr the falcon. They are the blessed ones in the god's company, and Ani asks to be fed as they are.

sentences.i: May a seat be made for me in the bark on the day the god crosses over,
sentences.n: iry·tw n·i 'may there be made for me' is the eye ir with two reeds, then t and w, the passive sḏm·tw·f again, and n·i; Budge prints it as one word, which is split here as in line 22. st 'seat, place' (seat, t, house). m wiꜣ 'in the bark': wiꜣ is the boat with a cabin, the god's bark. hrw 'day' is the shelter h, mouth r, sun and stroke, followed directly by its genitive: hrw ḏꜣ nṯr 'the day of the god's crossing'. ḏꜣ 'cross over water' is the fire-drill ḏꜣ with vulture ꜣ as complement and the boat as classifier; Budge's line numeral 26 is printed inside it. nṯr 'the god' (flag and seated god) is the subject of the crossing, since an infinitive takes its subject as a genitive. The crossing is the god's voyage by boat, perhaps the festival procession of his bark.

sentences.i: for the ka of the Osiris Ani.
sentences.n: The hymn ends as the offering formula of line 5 did: n kꜣ n Wsir ꜣny 'for the ka of the Osiris Ani' — all that was asked is for him. This time Ani has neither his title nor mꜣꜥ-ḫrw. Wsir is written with the eye and a low, long seat (coded Q2, an approximation of the type). After this line Budge prints, as an Appendix, a hymn to Ra from another papyrus (that of Nekht, British Museum 10471), which is not part of Ani's text and is left out.

glossary.ḏfꜣw: ḏfꜣw — food, provisions (noun m.; often paired with kꜣw)

glossary.wꜥ: wꜥ — one; (as a noun) one (of), someone
glossary.tmmw: tmmw — mankind, all people (noun m. plural; Budge: tememu)

glossary.imntt: imntt — the West, the realm of the dead
glossary.iꜣbtt: iꜣbtt — the east, the eastern quarter where the sun rises (noun f.)
glossary.ity: ity — sovereign, monarch (noun m.; title of a king, and of a god as ruler)
glossary.wḏꜣ: wḏꜣ — to proceed, go on, set out (verb) · a second word of the same spelling: to be sound, prosper (verb; ꜥnḫ wḏꜣ snb 'life, prosperity, health')
glossary.snb: snb — to be healthy, be well (verb); health (noun m.; the third word of ꜥnḫ wḏꜣ snb 'life, prosperity, health')
glossary.·tn: ·tn — you, your (2nd person plural suffix pronoun)
glossary.sw: sw — he, him, it (3rd person masculine singular dependent pronoun)
glossary.irw: irw — form, shape, appearance (noun m.; from iri 'do, make')
glossary.nfr: nfr — beautiful, good, perfect (adjective; follows its noun; verb 'be good'); also beauty, goodness (noun m.)
glossary.ꜥḏt: ꜥḏt — the sun's bark of the day, the morning bark (boat name; the reading follows the signs: the morning bark is usually named mꜥnḏt, also ꜥnḏt; Budge: āṭtet)
glossary.ḥry: ḥry — upper, who/which is above, upon (nisba of ḥr)
glossary.ẖry: ẖry — lower, who/which is beneath (nisba of ẖr)

glossary.·w: ·w — ending of the 3rd person masculine singular of the stative ('he is …ed'; often not written)
glossary.sḏt: sḏt — fire, flame (noun; written with the crossed sticks, sḏ)
glossary.sbiw: sbiw — rebel, the rebel serpent, enemy of the sun-god (noun m.; from sbi 'rebel'; Budge: Sebàu)
glossary.qꜣs: qꜣs — to bind, tie up (verb; stative 'bound')
glossary.nḥm: nḥm — to take away, carry off, snatch · also to rescue, save (from)
glossary.sḏm·n·f: sḏm·n·f — the n of the sḏm·n·f, marking a completed action ("I have …", "I …ed") (verb form; written between the verb and its suffix)
glossary.rd: rd — foot, leg (noun; dual rd·fy "his two feet") · a second word of the same spelling: to grow (verb)
glossary.msw: msw — children, offspring (noun; plural of ms 'child', from msi 'give birth')
glossary.bdš: bdš — to be weak, faint (verb); weakness (noun)
glossary.wnn: wnn — to be, exist (verb; wn·n·i "I have been"; n wn "there is not")
glossary.·sn: ·sn — they, them, their (3rd person plural suffix pronoun)
glossary.ḥwt-sr: ḥwt-sr — 'Mansion of the Noble', a sanctuary of the sun at Heliopolis (place name; Budge: ḥet ser)
glossary.nhm: nhm — to rejoice, shout for joy (verb); a shout of joy (noun)
glossary.st: st — place, seat, throne (noun) · a second word of the same spelling: it, them (3rd person dependent pronoun, object of a verb, written s-t)
glossary.wr: wr — great (adjective); a great one, a great amount (noun)
glossary.stwt: stwt — rays, beams of light, esp. of the sun (noun f. plural; Budge: satetu)
glossary.bꜥḥ: bꜥḥ — to flood, inundate, overflow (verb); the flood, inundation (noun m.)
glossary.ḥm: ḥm — majesty (noun; ḥm n N "the Majesty of N", of gods and kings)
glossary.pn: pn — this (masculine demonstrative, after its noun)
glossary.šps: šps — noble, august, venerable (adjective; follows its noun) · also rich, precious; a noble (noun)
glossary.ḫnm: ḫnm — to smell; to be joined with (verb); here, doubtfully, as a noun "companion, friend"
glossary.ḥḏ: ḥḏ — to damage, defraud, diminish · a second word of the same spelling: white, bright (adjective; verb 'be white, bright'; written with the mace)
glossary.mswt: mswt — birth, the being born (noun f.; from msi 'give birth')
glossary.pḥ: pḥ — to reach, arrive at, attain (verb)
glossary.·i: ·i — I, me (1st-person singular suffix pronoun; the seated-man sign)
glossary.nfrw: nfrw — beauty, goodness (noun; abstract plural of nfr "good, beautiful")
glossary.tp: tp — head, top; ḥry tp "who is upon" (noun)
glossary.ꜥꜣ: ꜥꜣ — great (adjective); (adverb) here, hither · a second word of the same spelling: donkey, ass (noun) · a third word of the same spelling: door, door-leaf (noun; iry-ꜥꜣ "doorkeeper")
glossary.bḥn: bḥn — to strike down, cut up, hack (verb)
glossary.sḥtm: sḥtm — to destroy, wipe out (verb; causative of ḥtm 'perish')
glossary.ꜥꜣpp: ꜥꜣpp — Apep, the great serpent, enemy of the sun-god (god's name; Budge: Āpep)
glossary.ꜣbḏw: ꜣbḏw — Abydos, the holy city of Osiris (place name; Budge: Àbṭu) · a second word of the same spelling: the abdju-fish (noun; a fish that swims before the sun's bark)
glossary.sp: sp — time, occasion; deed, case, matter (noun); sp sn 'twice'
glossary.ḫpr: ḫpr — to come into being, happen, become (verb)
glossary.int: int — the inet-fish, a kind of fish (noun) · a second word of the same spelling: valley, wadi (noun f.)
glossary.iry: iry — one who belongs to, keeper of (nisba of r "to"; iry ꜥꜣ "doorkeeper")
glossary.ḥmw: ḥmw — steering-oar, rudder (noun m.; Budge: ḥemu)
glossary.ḥꜣt: ḥꜣt — front, forepart, the prow of a boat; beginning (noun f.)
glossary.sktt: sktt — Sektet, the evening bark of the sun (boat name; Budge: sektet)
glossary.pḥwy: pḥwy — hinder parts, back, rear; end (noun)
glossary.itn: itn — the disk of the sun, the Aten (noun)
glossary.dgi: dgi — to look, look at, behold (verb; also written dgg)
glossary.iꜥḥ: iꜥḥ — the moon; Iah, the moon as a god (noun m.; god's name; Budge: Àḥ)
glossary.ꜣb: ꜣb — to cease, stop (verb; n ꜣbw 'without ceasing')
glossary.swtwt: swtwt — to stroll, walk about, go about (verb)
glossary.bw: bw — place (noun; bw mꜣꜥ "what is right", lit. "the place of right")
glossary.mri: mri — to love, wish, desire (verb; relative form mrrt·f, mrt·f 'what he loves, what he desires')
glossary.nis: nis — to call, summon, call out (a name) (verb)
glossary.sḏm·tw·f: sḏm·tw·f — the tw of the sḏm·tw·f, the passive or impersonal form ("one …", "… is done") (verb form; written after the verb, before its suffix)
glossary.ḫt: ḫt — thing, things, property (noun) · a second word of the same spelling: wood, tree, stick, a wooden board (noun m.)
glossary.wdb: wdb — to turn back, turn over, revert (verb); wdb ḫt 'the reversion of offerings', the passing on of offerings from the god to others (noun) · a second word of the same spelling: shore, riverbank (noun)
glossary.m-bꜣḥ: m-bꜣḥ — in the presence of, before (compound preposition: m 'in' + bꜣḥ 'presence', written with the phallus sign bꜣḥ)
glossary.mi: mi — come! (the imperative that serves the verbs of coming, iwi and ii; in later copies written with the owl m and the forearm ꜥ, as if mꜥ, with the walking legs) · a second word of the same spelling: like, as (preposition)
glossary.šmsw: šmsw — follower, attendant (noun; from šms 'to follow')
glossary.wiꜣ: wiꜣ — boat, bark, especially of a god (noun)
glossary.hrw: hrw — terror, dread · a second word of the same spelling: day (noun; plural hrww)
